chapter_title: Concerning the First Man and the Ambassador and the Ship; what they resemble.
chapter_note: This chapter is largely a set of internally-cosmological similes (First Man, Living Spirit, Great Spirit in the Ship, Ambassador) describing redemption within the Manichaean system. Only the final paragraph pivots into direct exhortation to disciples (application voice), marking a later pastoral graft. Paragraph 1 contains a clear hagiographic/frame attribution that must be stripped to recover the teaching.

paragraphs.core_text: The First [Man] is like a great distinguished man whose treasure has been taken away from him. He came to pursue his treasure. This is how the [First] Man too came after his sons from the heights, so that he might redeem them and retrieve his treasure, which had been scattered amongst his enemies.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed hagiographic/frame attribution: “Once again he speaks:” (dialogue/teaching-introduction formula).
paragraphs.temporal_note: The opening speech-attribution is a compiling-community frame marker; the remaining content is a cosmological simile mapping First Man’s descent and recovery of the Living Soul/treasure entirely within the Light–Darkness economy (cosmos→cosmos).

paragraphs.core_text: Once again, [he is like a man] whose two sons were taken away from him by [ ... He] came out toward them to redeem them. Again, this is how the First Man [ ... ] shines in the heights because of his two sons, who were separated from him. They are his living soul that exist in two powers, which makes four.
paragraphs.temporal_note: System-internal cosmological accounting (sons/living soul/powers) presented as a simile without institutional address, citation, or biographical praise; the mapping stays within the mythic-cosmic architecture despite the unclear numeration.

paragraphs.core_text: Once again, the ship [of the day] is like a great spear [ ... ... The Great Spirit too, which is in it, is like a wise [crafts]man who might beautify and set aright [all] the armour for war.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Pure correspondential simile: Ship of the Day and Great Spirit described by crafted-object/war-gear imagery (cosmos→cosmos), with no turn toward church practice or audience exhortation.

paragraphs.core_text: Once again, the Living Spirit is like a combatant who might go towards a king's son who has been taken prisoner of war, and he redeems him from the hands of his enemies.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal, mythic-redemptive mechanism stated as a simile (Living Spirit as rescuer) with no overlay citations or institutional application; reads as core teaching style.

paragraphs.core_text: [The Amba]ssador too is like a great man [ ... ] because of the treasure [ ... ] hand of his prisoners [ ... ] these light powers [ ... ... the] sons and their soul, so that they would [ ... ... (the soul) might] be brought forth in the land wherein it was imprisoned.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Despite lacunae, the content remains fully within the redemption-myth register (Ambassador, Light powers, imprisoned soul), not pointing outward to contemporary institutions; likely part of an older simile-collection.

Direct second-person exhortation (“You yourselves must be purifiers…”) addressed to disciples, aiming at membership/eschatological ‘counting’ and communal identity; this is application voice (cosmos→audience conduct) rather than system exposition.
